analysis.one_liner: Lets people wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans can only be wiped out in bankruptcy if the borrower proves the payments are an "undue hardship" — a very high bar that most borrowers cannot clear. This bill would remove that hurdle for private (non-government) student loans, letting people discharge them in bankruptcy the same way they can discharge credit card or medical debt. Federal student loans would still be protected. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers drowning in private student loan debt — people who took out loans from banks, Sallie Mae/Navient-type lenders, or school-financing programs and now cannot pay. It would give them a real escape hatch in bankruptcy instead of a lifetime of collection. It would also apply to future bankruptcy cases only, so it would not reopen old cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private student loan borrowers in bankruptcy

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the special bankruptcy protection that private student loans currently enjoy: today a borrower must prove an 'undue hardship' to discharge any student loan, and this bill removes that requirement for private loans, making them dischargeable like credit card or medical debt [S2] [S3].
The change covers private loans and loans from programs not funded by the government, while leaving federally backed student loans' special treatment in place [S3].
It applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after the bill became law, so borrowers would get a clear, predictable rule going forward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders and debt collectors who buy this debt. Loans they currently can pursue for decades with garnishment and no bankruptcy escape would become collectible only for as long as the borrower stays out of bankruptcy, so they would expect bigger losses on defaulted loans. Future borrowers might face somewhat higher rates or tighter credit from these lenders as a result.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student lenders and debt buyers

drawbacks.text: Because the loans would become dischargeable, private lenders would likely charge higher interest rates or lend less, especially to students at schools with weak outcomes — the standard trade-off of any bankruptcy relief, since lenders price in the loans they cannot collect [S2] [S3].

The bill does nothing for the far larger group holding federal student loans, who would still face the 'undue hardship' hurdle, so the people most likely to be helped are those who borrowed from private lenders rather than the government [S2] [S3].

There is no income targeting: an affluent borrower with a temporary setback could use bankruptcy to shed private loan debt just as a truly struggling one could, which is the same rule as for credit cards but a real cost critics would point to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific, badly hurting group: borrowers whose private loans would otherwise follow them for life even after a bankruptcy filing. The costs — somewhat higher private loan rates and a windfall for some borrowers who could have repaid — are real but modest, and the same trade-off society already accepts for credit cards and medical bills. The bill's narrowness is its main design weakness: it leaves federal borrowers, the majority of student debtors, under the old rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Private Student Loan Bankruptcy Fairness Act of 2023 on January 9, 2023, with four Democratic cosponsors joining at introduction [S1] [S4].
That same day it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — the standard first step, which puts the bill in a committee's hands and off the floor until that committee acts [S5].

No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote. The action history ends with the referral, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders and debt collectors are better off, because the bankruptcy protection that makes these loans collectible for decades remains in place. Borrowers with private loans gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; has filed versions of this bill in prior Congresses.

for.name: Reps. Danny Davis, Eric Swalwell, Julia Brownley, and Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; its action history ends at referral [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Set the agenda for the chamber and never brought the bill to the floor; the party controls which bills get committee time.

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.role: Lenders and debt buyers with the special bankruptcy protection at stake
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed comparable bankruptcy-reform bills in prior Congresses; no industry lobbying appears in this bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: All six members behind the bill were Democrats; the bill went to a committee chaired by a Republican in a Republican-controlled House and never advanced, with no Republican support at any point.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders (banks and non-bank lenders such as Sallie Mae/Navient)
industries.note: These lenders' loans are among the few consumer debts that survive bankruptcy, letting them pursue borrowers for decades through garnishment and collection suits. The bill would strip that protection, making defaulted loans collectible only until a borrower files bankruptcy.

industries.industry: Debt buyers and collection agencies holding private student loan paper
industries.note: Much old private student debt is bought and worked by collectors precisely because it cannot be discharged. The bill would make that debt worth less, cutting into the value of what they buy.
Easier discharge of private student loans would create more work and clearer filings for bankruptcy practitioners representing individual debtors.
